newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Golkar heads for expected victory.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Golkar heads for expected victory.

text.p: Indonesia's ruling Golkar, assured of victory even before a vote was cast, headed for a landslide win on Friday after the most violent general election campaign in three decades.

With more than half the potential ballots counted, Golkar's main rival, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) also saw its share of the vote rise in Thursday's voting for 425 elected seats in the House of Representatives.
But there was renewed violence on Thursday night, with police reporting that a mob rampaged through the town of Sampang on Madura, a strongly-Moslem island off Java's east coast.
The mob, angered by Golkar's election gains in a PPP stronghold, burned dozens of homes in a teachers' housing complex.
"It's quiet again today after last night's disturbances," a policeman said by phone from Sampang.
There were no reports, however, of trouble in Jakarta or Central Java, where much of the election campaign violence occurred.

In the former Portuguese colony of East Timor, at least 14 people died in a wave of election violence, with the casualties including a soldier killed by rebels on Thursday while guarding a polling booth.

The big loser in the elections was the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), badly split after Megawati Sukarnoputri, eldest daughter of Indonesia's founding president Sukarno, was ousted as party leader by a government-backed rival last year.
Political analysts said the interest in the poll lay in the size of Golkar's victory, whether PPP supporters were satisfied with their share and the rate of spoiled ballots and abstentions.

Election officials gave Golkar just over 70 million of the roughly 96 million votes counted by 10.30 a.m. (0330 GMT), or 73.46 percent. The PPP had around 23 million votes or 23.68 percent, and the PDI 2.7 million votes or 2.86 percent.
"It seems that Golkar will have its heart's wish, it will probably have a landslide," said analyst Dewi Fortuna Anwar of the Centre for Information and Development Studies (CIDES).

Diplomatic sources said President Suharto had pushed for a strong showing for Golkar as an endorsement of government policies. Golkar officials had said they were looking for just over 70 percent of the vote.
In the last elections in 1992, Golkar took 68 percent of the overall vote, the PPP 17 percent and the PDI 15 percent. Golkar's biggest win to date was 73.17 percent in 1987.
A foreign analyst closely monitoring Thursday's election, in which nearly 125 million people were eligible to vote, saw nothing unexpected in the Golkar tally.
"However, nobody expected the PDI vote to collapse like this," he said.
Political and financial market analysts had expressed apprehension that PPP supporters might take to the streets, particularly in Jakarta, if they felt they had been cheated in the election.

Analyst Dewi Anwar told Reuters she believed the election to have been generally free, but added that the two minority parties believed the system was stacked against them and heavily favoured Golkar.

"In terms of the election itself, I think it's free, so it is not the election itself that is the problem. If Golkar wins, I don't think it will be bacause of vote manipulation or anything like that," she said.
"It's just that conditions are made which means it is quite hard for Golkar to loose."
